request: Bank statements for all accounts, every month of the period
why: To verify the company's cash balances throughout the year and confirm they agree with the bank's records, we need to see each account's activity and balances.
good_looks_like: A bank statement for every account the company held during the year, covering each month of the period. Each statement should show the opening balance, transactions, and closing balance. Download them as PDFs from online banking; photos or scans are harder to read.

why: To confirm that the company's cash balance in the accounting system matches what the bank records show at year end, and to explain any differences.
good_looks_like: A bank reconciliation for each account as of the year-end date, showing the bank's closing balance, the accounting system balance, and a line-by-line list of items that explain the difference (such as cheques not yet cleared or deposits not yet processed). The total should agree with your accounting system.

why: To confirm the cash the company held at year end, we compare each bank account's balance with the bank's own record.
good_looks_like: A bank confirmation letter from each bank where the company holds an account, dated at or shortly after the year-end date. The letter should come directly from the bank on its letterhead and show the account number, the balance at year end, and any authorized signatories. If the bank won't send a letter, a bank statement for each account covering the year-end date with opening and closing balances will work instead.

why: To confirm the petty cash the company held at year end matches your accounting records and that the cash physically exists.
good_looks_like: A record of the petty cash count performed at or very close to the year-end date, showing the amount counted, who counted it, the date and time of the count, and confirmation it agrees with your accounting system.

request: Accounts receivable aging at period end
why: To see who owes the company money at year end and for how long, and to check it agrees with your accounting system.
good_looks_like: An aged receivables report as of the year-end date, by customer, with totals by age band (for example, current, 30 days overdue, 60 days overdue, 90+ days overdue), exported from your accounting system without edits.

why: To confirm that amounts customers owed at year end were genuine, we check whether the company received payment after year end.
good_looks_like: A report or spreadsheet showing amounts received from customers in the period after the year-end date, matched to invoices or customer accounts from year end. Include the customer name, invoice date, amount received, and date of receipt.

why: To verify the allowance for doubtful accounts is calculated correctly and supported by evidence of which receivables may not be collected.
good_looks_like: A spreadsheet showing how the allowance was calculated at the year-end date. Include the method used (such as a percentage of sales, aging analysis, or individual customer assessment), the receivables or customer balances it applies to, and the resulting allowance amount. The total should agree with your accounting system.

request: Accounts payable aging at period end
why: To see what the company owed its suppliers at year end and confirm nothing is missing.
good_looks_like: An aged payables report as of the year-end date, by supplier, with totals by age band, exported from your accounting system without edits.

why: To check that all amounts the company owed at year end are recorded in the accounts, we need to see the evidence you used to search for any liabilities that might have been missed.
good_looks_like: Documentation of your search for unrecorded liabilities, such as: a list of suppliers contacted after year end to confirm amounts owed; bank statements and credit card statements for the period after year end showing payments made; correspondence with creditors; or a summary of procedures performed to identify any invoices received after year end for goods or services provided before year end. Include dates and amounts where relevant.

why: To see what costs the company has incurred but not yet paid at year end, and to confirm the accrual is complete and accurate.
good_looks_like: A spreadsheet listing each accrued expense item at the year-end date, with descriptions, amounts, and the total that agrees with your accounting system. Include the supplier or cost category for each item.

why: To verify the inventory quantities the company recorded at year end, we need to see how the physical count was performed and what was found.
good_looks_like: Documentation of the inventory count process, including the date(s) it took place, the locations counted, the method used (such as full count or cycle count), and the results showing quantities by item or location. This should tie to the inventory balance in your accounting system at year end. Provide count sheets, reconciliations, or a summary report in spreadsheet or document form.

why: To confirm how the company values its inventory at year end and that the cost is accurate, we need to understand the methods used and see the calculations behind the reported balance.
good_looks_like: A summary of the inventory valuation methods used (such as first-in-first-out, weighted average, or standard cost), any adjustments made at year end (for obsolescence, damage or slow-moving stock), and a spreadsheet showing how the final inventory balance was calculated and agreed to the accounting system.

why: To see how the company's property and equipment balance changed during the year, including additions, disposals, and depreciation, and to confirm it agrees with your accounting system.
good_looks_like: A spreadsheet showing each asset or asset category with its opening balance at the start of the year, additions and disposals during the year, depreciation charged, and closing balance at the year-end date. Include a total row that agrees with your accounting system.

request: Invoices for fixed asset additions over the threshold
why: To verify that fixed asset additions recorded in your accounts are genuine, properly valued, and correctly classified.
good_looks_like: Copies of invoices for all fixed asset purchases above your capitalization threshold during the year, showing the vendor, description of the asset, purchase date, and amount. Invoices should be in their original form (PDF or scanned) and cover the full year.

why: To verify that depreciation expense for the year is calculated correctly and that accumulated depreciation on the balance sheet is accurate.
good_looks_like: A spreadsheet showing each asset or asset category, its cost, useful life in years, depreciation method (such as straight-line), opening accumulated depreciation, depreciation charged for the year, and closing accumulated depreciation as of the year-end date. The total closing accumulated depreciation should agree with your accounting system.

why: To understand the terms of the company's debt, including interest rates, repayment schedules and any covenants, and to confirm the year-end balance is complete and accurate.
good_looks_like: Copies of all debt agreements in place at year end, including loan agreements, credit facilities and any bonds or notes issued. Include any amendments or side letters signed during the year that change the original terms. Provide the documents as they were signed, or as updated if formally amended.

why: To verify the company complied with its debt covenants at year end and understand any waivers or breaches that may affect the financial statements.
good_looks_like: A spreadsheet or document showing each debt covenant, the calculation method, the actual result at the year-end date, the required threshold, and whether it was met. Include the source of each figure (such as the accounting system or loan agreement) and any covenant waivers or amendments signed during the year.

why: To verify that interest expense recorded in the year is accurate and complete, we recalculate it from the underlying debt agreements and balances.
good_looks_like: A spreadsheet showing each debt facility held during the year, with the interest rate, opening and closing balances, and the interest expense calculated for the year. Include a total that agrees with the interest expense in your accounting system at year end.

why: To understand the company's ownership structure at year end and verify that share issuances, repurchases, and transfers are recorded correctly in the accounting system.
good_looks_like: A spreadsheet or document showing each shareholder's name, number of shares held, share class, and percentage ownership as of the year-end date. Include a summary of all share transactions during the year (issuances, repurchases, transfers) with dates and quantities. The total shares outstanding should agree with your accounting system.

why: To confirm that any dividends paid or declared during the year were properly authorized by the board before payment or announcement.
good_looks_like: Board minutes or resolutions from board meetings held during the year that document approval of dividends, including the date approved, amount per share, and payment date. If dividends were declared after year end but relate to the year, include those approvals too.

why: To understand the terms of your significant customer contracts and confirm revenue is recognized correctly and completely at year end.
good_looks_like: Copies of the signed contracts for each significant customer, showing the key terms: what goods or services are provided, the price, payment terms, and any conditions that affect when revenue should be recognized (such as performance milestones or return rights). If contracts are very long, a summary of these key points is acceptable.

why: To confirm that sales are recorded in the correct period, we test transactions around the year-end date to ensure revenue is recognized when goods or services are delivered, not when the invoice is sent or payment is received.
good_looks_like: A list of sales transactions from a few days before and after the year-end date, showing the invoice date, delivery date, and amount for each. Include enough detail to let us trace each transaction back to your accounting system and supporting documents like delivery notes or customer confirmations.

why: To understand how deferred revenue changed during the year and confirm the year-end balance is accurate and complete.
good_looks_like: A spreadsheet showing deferred revenue by type or contract, with opening balance at the start of the year, amounts received or recognized during the year, and closing balance at the year-end date. The closing balance should agree with your accounting system.

request: Payroll registers for two pay periods
why: To verify the payroll costs recorded in your accounts and check that employee deductions and employer contributions are correct.
good_looks_like: The payroll register for each of the two pay periods, showing gross pay, all deductions (tax, social security, pension, etc.), net pay, and employer contributions by employee. Export directly from your payroll system without edits, and confirm the totals agree with your accounting records for those periods.

why: To verify the payroll taxes the company reported and paid to tax authorities during the year, and to check they agree with your payroll records.
good_looks_like: Copies of all quarterly payroll tax returns filed for the year, as submitted to the relevant tax authority. Include the filing confirmation or receipt showing the date filed and any reference number.

why: To verify that bonuses owed to employees at year end are complete and accurate, and that the accrual in your accounts is correct.
good_looks_like: A spreadsheet or document showing how the bonus accrual was calculated at the year-end date: the employees eligible, the bonus amount or formula for each, and the total accrued. It should tie to your payroll records and accounting system.

why: To identify all leases the company is party to and understand their key terms, we need to review the agreements themselves.
good_looks_like: Copies of all lease agreements in effect at the year-end date or signed during the year, including any amendments or side letters. Include leases for property, equipment, vehicles or other assets, whether the company is the lessee or lessor. Provide them as PDFs or scans, ideally organized by asset type or lease commencement date.

request: Lease liability and right-of-use asset schedule
why: To see what leases the company has, their key terms, and how the lease liability and right-of-use asset are calculated at year end.
good_looks_like: A spreadsheet listing each lease, with columns for the lease term, commencement date, payment amounts, discount rate used, and the resulting lease liability and right-of-use asset balance as of the year-end date. Include a total row that agrees with your accounting system.

why: To identify any legal claims, disputes or obligations the company faces that may need to be recorded or disclosed in the financial statements.
good_looks_like: A letter from each law firm or legal advisor the company uses, dated at or shortly after the year-end date, confirming the status of any pending or threatened litigation, claims, or legal matters. The letter should describe each matter, its likely outcome, and any estimated financial exposure. If there are no matters, the letter should confirm that too.

why: To verify the insurance policies the company has in place at year end and confirm the prepaid insurance balance is accurate and supported.
good_looks_like: Copies of all active insurance policies and certificates as of the year-end date, showing the policyholder, coverage type, coverage period, premium amount, and renewal date. Include any endorsements or amendments. Provide them as PDFs or scans, organized by policy type.
